messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos, a 28-year-old Latin American prison guard, had been married only a few years when his older brother died suddenly and violently in an unexpected incident that tore through the family with no warning. One day his brother was there, joking in the kitchen over coffee, and the next Carlos was standing in a hospital corridor hearing words he could not take in, then later watching relatives gather in stunned silence while his mother repeated his name as if repetition might bring him back. After that, ordinary moments began to feel dangerous in a way he could not explain to his wife or coworkers. When a news clip about a fatal accident came on in the break room, or when someone at work casually talked about people losing loved ones, he would feel a strange detached, unreal quality settle over him, as if he were standing a little outside his own body watching everything through glass. Those moments did not just upset him; they made him feel that the loss was everywhere, waiting for him in the next headline or conversation, and he would immediately shove the feeling away by covering his face with his hands, leaving the room, or creating drama with whoever was nearest so he would not have to sit with the grief. He came to avoid anything that reminded him of someone he had lost, including the kind of music his brother liked and family gatherings where his brother’s absence was obvious.

What Carlos told himself about these reactions made everything feel worse. He had become convinced that he was no longer the happy person he used to be and that now he was always miserable, and he carried a bleak sense that he had no future that could feel intact or worth wanting. Beneath that was the harsher thought that he should have protected others and failed, a belief that settled on him whenever he remembered how helpless he had felt at the hospital and how little he could do to change what had happened. That judgment did not stay contained; it made every reminder of loss feel like evidence against him. A conversation about someone losing a loved one, a condolence card, or a news story about sudden death would immediately pull him back into the same conviction that he had failed once already and could fail again. In those moments he would hide his face, leave the scene, or pick a fight at home, not only to escape the pain but because the misery and shame seemed too big to hold quietly.

Over the months, the habits began to tighten around him. At home with his wife, he would sometimes start arguments over small things, almost as if he needed noise and conflict to outrun the stillness that arrived whenever the house reminded him of his brother. At work in the prison, where death and loss were sometimes discussed in the blunt language of staff rooms and corridors, he found himself scanning news feeds on his phone with dread, only to regret it and react by snapping at a coworker or stirring up unnecessary conflict to push the feeling away. Yet those outbursts left him more ashamed and more certain that he had become a man who could not hold himself together. The more he acted this way, the more he returned to the same thought that he was miserable and had no future, and the more any mention of death, any story of a family member lost, seemed to strike straight at that belief and set off the unreal, detached feeling again. He had learned to dread those moments precisely because they carried him back into the proof, in his mind, that he had failed and that loss would keep finding him.

By the time he sought help, Carlos was exhausted by the cycle and frightened by how quickly he could shift from numbness to anger to shame. He wanted to stop hiding his face, stop provoking fights, and stop turning away from anything that might remind him of the brother he lost, but he was also afraid that if he let himself grieve, he would be swallowed by the certainty that he had no future and that the man he used to be was gone for good.
